entries.answer: A database stores data so it can be found again later, unlike a file which has to be read end to end. A relational database keeps data in tables of rows and columns, and you ask it questions with SQL, a language designed for exactly that. The point is not speed alone but that data stays consistent when many things read and write at once.

entries.answer: SQL is the language for asking a relational database questions in a declarative way, meaning you state the result you want rather than the steps to get it. The database works out the steps, which is the whole point and also the trap, because a perfectly clear query can still be catastrophically slow. Learning to read an execution plan matters more than memorising syntax.

patterns: do i need a primary key
entries.answer: A primary key is the column or set of columns that uniquely identifies a row, and it is enforced rather than trusted. That enforcement is its real value, because an application that guesses a key is fine until two people guess the same one. An auto-incrementing integer is the usual choice, and a composite key using two columns is the answer when no single column is unique alone.

patterns: what does on delete cascade do
entries.answer: A foreign key is a column that references the primary key of another table, and it stops a row pointing at something that does not exist. Without it, the references in your data are a convention only the application enforces, so a bug in one screen quietly breaks every other. The cost is that deleting a referenced row now needs a decision about what happens to the rows pointing at it.

entries.answer: Normalization organises tables so each fact is stored once, which removes contradictions where two copies disagree and makes updates safe. The first three normal forms cover repeating groups, partial dependencies and transitive dependencies. It is not free, because every join costs something at read time, so denormalising a hot read-heavy table is a deliberate choice rather than a mistake.

patterns: difference between inner and left join
what does a left join do
why is my left join returning too many rows
entries.answer: A join combines rows from two tables on a shared column, and the type of join decides what happens to rows that do not match. An inner join keeps only matching rows, a left join keeps everything from the left with nulls for the rest, and a full join keeps both. The left join causes most surprise, because switching an inner for a left silently multiplies rows on a many-to-one relationship.

patterns: why is my index not used
entries.answer: An index is a separate structure that lets the database find rows without reading the whole table, trading write speed and disk for read speed. It is worth having on columns you filter, join or sort by, and worth not having on a small table where a full scan is already cheap. The common failure is indexing a low-selectivity column, since an index on a boolean often costs more to maintain than the scan it replaces.

entries.answer: A transaction groups statements so they all succeed or all fail together, which is what stops a half-finished transfer from existing. The properties are called ACID: atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability. The isolation level is the dial that matters in practice, because it decides whether a concurrent read can see partially applied work.

patterns: when to use nosql instead of sql
entries.answer: NoSQL covers database families that give up some relational guarantees in exchange for horizontal scaling and flexible structure. Document stores keep JSON-like records, key-value stores are a fast lookup table, and column and graph stores suit different access patterns. The honest tradeoff is that these scale more easily but corrupt more easily, because no schema stops a field from being missing or the wrong type.
